deep_why: The paper computes the worst-case additive distance between what an online policy achieves and what an oracle could do with perfect foresight. The soundness rests on measuring regret under full knowledge of values in [0,1]—this creates a bounded problem space where no policy can exceed 1 unit of loss. Pricing-curve algorithms work because they treat the secretary selection as a continuous threshold problem: by pricing candidates relative to the running best seen so far, they exploit the statistical structure that later arrivals have a roughly fixed chance of surpassing any threshold. This principle holds because arrivals are uniformly random, so the ranking order is independent of values, letting a simple pricing rule match the worst-case optimally. The tighter regret bounds matter because online hiring happens once, and knowing you'll never be more than 0.25 away from optimal provides concrete assurance in practice.

The paper measures how easily one class of examples gets mislabeled as another class during attack. The vulnerability fundamentally stems from class overlap: when true examples near the decision boundary between two classes become similar in the feature space, flipping a label from one class to the other creates less of a contradiction for the model to learn. Classes with high confusability (small separation) thus require less label noise to corrupt model behavior. The defense works by explicitly pushing apart the two most vulnerable class pairs in the feature space, which directly increases the margin an attacker must overcome. This is sound because a model trained on more separated classes must move decision boundaries farther to accommodate mislabeled examples, making the attack less effective. The approach connects to practice because it protects where attacks do maximum damage—not all classes equally.

The paper compresses large datasets into small synthetic ones that train different model architectures equally well. The core challenge is that a synthetic dataset tuned to one architecture (say, a convolutional design) learns to exploit that architecture's specific inductive biases, becoming useless for another architecture (a vision transformer). The paper casts this as an information problem: the synthetic data should carry only the core knowledge needed for the task, not extra information tightly coupled to the source architecture. By treating the problem as a game where one player minimizes the information the synthetic data reveals about which architecture was used, they force the synthetic examples to be architecture-agnostic. This works because information-theoretic mutual information captures exactly when two things are dependent—removing it ensures the data remains useful regardless of architectural choice. The result saves computation because one distilled dataset now serves many model types.

The paper organizes fairness in information retrieval using economic principles: viewing the Web ecosystem as a market with producers (publishers), consumers (searchers), and intermediaries (the search system itself). This lens is sound because both economics and retrieval systems solve the same fundamental problem—allocating limited attention or visibility to heterogeneous entities with competing interests. By mapping fairness concerns onto established economic dimensions (macro/micro, demand/supply, temporal), the framework provides a structured vocabulary for talking about fairness trade-offs. For instance, a policy that increases visibility for under-represented sources helps at the macro level but may decrease utility for individual searchers. The economic perspective works because it inherits centuries of thinking about when allocation mechanisms are fair and to whom, applying those insights directly to retrieval fairness.

The paper tracks the stability of fact-check annotations after they become visible to raters. The core finding is that helpful notes lose consensus after display because raters with opposing viewpoints begin voting against them. This instability is inevitable because visibility triggers selective participation: people who disagree are now motivated to rate, while the original consensus was built in the absence of that opposition. The underlying principle is that consensus in a limited sample can be unstable when the broader population holds different views—once you expand who can vote, the old consensus breaks. Community-based systems are vulnerable to this because they depend on sufficient agreement, which collapses when polarization drives counter-voting. Understanding this mechanism matters because it reveals why consensus-based moderation systems cannot simply display notes and expect them to persist; they must account for how visibility changes the voting incentives.

The paper detects anomalies in sensor streams by splitting the task: lightweight edge screening identifies candidates quickly, then cloud verification with larger models confirms real anomalies with explanations. The soundness comes from asymmetry in error cost—false alarms at the edge are cheap (quick filtering) while missed anomalies are expensive, but once an edge alert arrives, the cloud can afford to spend resources on confirmation and reasoning. This two-stage design is sound because most sensor data is normal, so an edge model catching 90% of anomalies with many false positives is still useful; the cloud refines down to truly anomalous cases. The principle applies because the cloud has latency-tolerance and the edge has compute limits, so dividing by urgency (screen now, analyze later) is natural. Interpretability through explanation generation then closes the loop—operators need to understand why something flagged, not just that it did.

The paper compresses a text-attributed graph (nodes with descriptions plus edges) into a tiny synthetic version that still trains the model accurately. The approach works in two parts: first, it selects representative text snippets from related nodes by maximizing mutual information, ensuring selected texts capture maximum unique signal about the graph structure. Second, it aligns synthetic similarities to match the real data's similarity structure, which is more stable than aligning individual trajectories during training. The principle is that if the model learns to rely on which texts look similar and which nodes connect, then preserving those two geometric structures preserves what matters. This is sound because similarities and connectivity are low-variance properties compared to the high-variance training dynamics—a synthetic dataset matching these properties will generalize. The 1% compression becomes feasible because you're keeping only the structural fingerprint, not all original content.

The paper generates search queries directly from news posts using a language model, then scores by engagement and creator authority to surface trends before search volume accumulates. The soundness rests on the observation that trends emerge when many users shift attention simultaneously; by generating what they would search for, you detect that shift earlier than keyword frequency allows. The model must continually adapt as news and language evolve, but simple fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of prior knowledge. The paper addresses this by mixing on-policy stability (keep prior reasoning ability) with off-policy learning from new examples, preventing the model from unlearning old patterns while acquiring new ones. This dual objective works because trends are local novelties atop stable search behavior—you need both to catch long-tail shifts while remaining reliable. The mechanism matters operationally because it moves trend detection from reactive (waiting for queries) to proactive (generating them from content).

The paper generates video captions by building a multimodal graph that connects visual frames and text tokens through learned concept anchors, then guiding caption generation with diffusion conditioned on this graph structure. The core insight is that captions require understanding correlations across visual and textual modalities simultaneously, not in isolation. The graph-based approach is sound because it makes relational structure explicit—the model can reason about which visual concepts relate to which text fragments through explicit edges. Diffusion models are suitable for generation here because they gradually refine noisy text into coherent captions while respecting the graph structure as a constraint, balancing fidelity to the conditioning (the graph) with naturalness of output. The soft pruning of low-quality nodes further refines the graph by removing noise, leaving only reliable semantic relationships to guide generation. This works in practice because video captioning truly is a relational problem—describing what you see requires knowing how visual and textual content interrelate.

The paper evaluates temporal prediction methods on blockchain transaction data where outcomes depend on time-dependent factors (user churn, risk evolution) that violate standard independent-and-identically-distributed assumptions. The benchmark operationalizes real-world challenges by encoding censoring (some users drop out) and non-stationarity (user behavior shifts over extended periods) directly into 16 prediction tasks. The soundness is that blockchain data provides a clean, immutable, time-stamped event log with ground truth—you can replay history and measure exactly when a method would have made its prediction and whether it proved right. Methods that succeed here handle temporal reasoning without assuming the world is static, which few generic models do. The benchmark matters because Web3 systems are naturally temporal and decentralized in a way traditional Web domains are not, providing a high-fidelity testbed for temporal challenges that affect all temporal forecasting.

The system generates travel itineraries by scraping live travel content, summarizing it with a fine-tuned model, and composing structured plans using an accessible language model guided by user preference sliders. The approach works because each stage decouples a hard problem: scraping finds fresh data cheaply, summarization compresses it to essential facts, and slider-guided generation lets users control emphasis without complex instruction engineering. The architecture is sound because it respects the constraint that in-browser execution must be fast and privacy-preserving—by doing heavy lifting server-side (scraping, summarization) and lightweight generation client-side, the system balances freshness (you always see current content) with responsiveness (generation is fast). Preference sliders work because they translate nebulous user intent into numerical guidance the model can follow consistently, making interactive iteration practical. The demonstration shows the end-to-end Web intelligence pipeline—from acquisition to reasoning to human control.

The paper estimates how many distinct peers a host connects to using a compact sketch, but refines the estimate by respecting network topology: hosts talking within the same subnet are grouped separately from hosts crossing subnets. The soundness comes from the fact that super hosts attacking or compromised show a signature—they contact many peers, but those peers often lie in a few subnets (same organization or region). A traditional cardinality estimator treats all peer addresses equally, missing this structure, so it counts unique targets across the entire space and generates false alarms. By segmenting by subnet prefix, the approach aligns the estimation with the attack pattern: you measure cardinality within subnets, catching coordinated communication more accurately. The halved-segment hashing mechanism is sound because IP prefixes form a hierarchy—knowing the common prefix length between addresses tells you if they share a subnet. Using this to guide the sketch's memory allocation means you pay more attention to the levels where attacks cluster, improving detection precision while staying memory-efficient.

The paper adapts language models to graph tasks like node classification when labeled data is scarce by using semi-supervised learning: train on rare labeled examples, then iteratively generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled nodes and retrain. The soundness rests on the fact that graph structure itself conveys information—nodes with similar neighbors tend to have similar labels, a principle called homophily. By using edges to propagate information from labeled to unlabeled nodes through the model's own predictions, you leverage this structure without needing more manual annotations. The approach is sound because each iteration improves the pseudo-labels by training on an enlarged labeled set, and graph homophily means errors stay localized—a mislabeled node affects mostly its neighbors, not the entire dataset. Iterative self-training amplifies the signal because early iterations correct obvious mistakes, and later iterations refine edge cases. The method works in social domains where obtaining ground truth labels is expensive but graph structure is abundant and reliable.

The paper examines whether NFTs truly achieve decentralization by mapping real assets to their actual storage locations, revealing widespread reliance on fragile centralized services. The analysis is sound because immutability and decentralization are engineering properties that can be empirically verified—if most high-value NFTs point to off-chain servers that can be deleted or modified, the promise of permanence is false. The paper proposes a taxonomy of storage defects (access failure, tamperability, forgeability) that maps technical vulnerabilities to real risks. Each defect class corresponds to a failure mode: an inaccessible server breaks access, a modifiable server enables tampering, and a forgeable signature enables forgery. Quantifying severity with CVSS provides a structured risk assessment that practitioners can use. The contribution is sound because it bridges the gap between technical implementation and the promises made to users—showing empirically that the system falls short and providing a framework for improvement.

The paper blocks ads and trackers using hard-to-perturb features extracted from code and URL embeddings, then maintains accuracy over time through cheap pseudo-labeling instead of costly retraining. The core principle is that code and URL structure contain invariant patterns attackers struggle to change without breaking functionality—an attacker can tweak behavior to evade simple classifiers, but modifying code logic or URL structure usually breaks the ad or tracker's operation. Using learned embeddings of these features captures these invariants more robustly than hand-crafted rules. The system is sound because adversarial robustness arises naturally from features tied to functionality: if perturbing a feature breaks the actual attack, the classifier benefits automatically. Pseudo-labeling maintenance works because the classifier only needs occasional retraining on fresh examples to stay accurate; perfect accuracy is unnecessary if false positives are tolerable. The client-side architecture is sound for privacy because all decision-making happens locally, never transmitting URLs or scripts to external servers.
